Chapter 1: Data Collection

What This Chapter Is About
Good statistics starts with good data. Before any analysis, you need to know where your data came from, how it was collected, and whether it is representative of the population you care about. In agricultural economics, this means understanding farm surveys, USDA datasets, and sampling designs for crop yield studies.


The Process of Statistics
Every statistical study follows four steps:

Identify the research objective — What question are you answering? (Example: “What is the mean cotton yield on Lubbock County farms this season?”)
Collect data — Design a study and gather observations from a sample of the population.
Organize and summarize — Build frequency tables, compute averages, and draw graphs (Chapters 2–3).
Draw conclusions — Use inferential methods to generalize from the sample to the population (Chapters 8–11).

A population is the complete set of all individuals of interest. A sample is the subset actually observed. Because studying an entire population is usually impractical, we study a sample and use statistics to make inferences about the population.


Types of Variables
Before collecting data, identify the type of variable — this determines which formulas and graphs apply.

Rule of thumb: if you count to get the value → discrete; if you measure → continuous.


Sampling Methods








Method
How it works
When to use




Simple random
Every individual has an equal chance of selection
General surveys with a complete list (frame)


Stratified
Divide population into groups (strata); sample randomly within each
When subgroups (farm sizes, crop types) differ from one another


Systematic
Select every k-th individual; k = N/n
When a frame exists and ordering is random


Cluster
Randomly select groups (clusters); survey all members
When travel cost is high and clusters resemble the full population

Types of Sampling Designs

Simple random sampling: Every unit has an equal chance — use RAND() as above.
Stratified sampling: Divide farms by size (small, medium, large), then sample randomly within each stratum using RANDBETWEEN.
Systematic sampling: Select every kth farm from a sorted list. Compute k = N/n (e.g., every 7th farm if N=200, n=30).



Common Mistake
Using RAND() without freezing the value means your sample changes every time Excel recalculates. Always paste as Values Only before sorting.

section: Chapter 2: Summarizing Data in Tables and Graphs
text:
Chapter 2: Summarizing Data in Tables and Graphs

What This Chapter Is About
Raw numbers are hard to interpret. Frequency distributions, bar charts, and histograms compress hundreds of observations into patterns you can communicate and act on.


Frequency Distributions
A frequency distribution table organizes data into categories (qualitative) or equal-width intervals (quantitative) and counts how many observations fall in each group.
Relative frequency converts raw counts into proportions so you can compare distributions of different sizes:
\[\text{Relative frequency} = \frac{\text{frequency (count in class)}}{\sum \text{all frequencies}} = \frac{f}{\sum f}\]
Example: If 28 of 80 farms grow Cotton, the relative frequency = 28/80 = 0.35 (35%).
The sum of all relative frequencies must equal exactly 1 (or 100%).
Terms for grouped quantitative data:







Term
Definition




Class
An interval of values (e.g., 800–900 lbs/acre)


Lower class limit
Smallest value belonging to the class


Upper class limit
Largest value belonging to the class


Class width
Lower limit of next class − lower limit of this class


Class midpoint
(Lower limit + Upper limit) / 2 — represents the class in calculations


Cumulative frequency
Running total of frequencies up through a class





Types of Graphs








Graph
Data type
Key rule




Bar chart
Qualitative (categories)
Bars do not touch; order doesn’t matter


Histogram
Quantitative (grouped)
Bars do touch (no gaps); intervals are equal


Frequency polygon
Quantitative (grouped)
Connect midpoints with line segments; close to x-axis at both ends


Stem-and-leaf
Quantitative (raw)
Preserves original data values; quick to construct by hand

Shapes to Recognize

Symmetric / Bell-shaped: values cluster around the center.
Right-skewed: long tail to the right — common in farm income data.
Left-skewed: long tail to the left.
Bimodal: two peaks — may indicate two sub-populations (irrigated vs. dryland).

Chapter 3: Numerically Summarizing Data

What This Chapter Is About
A single number can summarize a whole distribution. This chapter covers measures of center (mean, median, mode) and spread (standard deviation, variance, IQR). Excel’s Descriptive Statistics tool generates all of them at once.


Measures of Central Tendency
(1) Mean — the arithmetic average; the balancing point of the data.
\[\mu = \frac{\sum X_i}{N} \quad \text{(population mean, } N \text{ = population size)}\]
\[\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n} \quad \text{(sample mean, } n \text{ = sample size)}\]
A key property: the sum of all deviations from the mean is always exactly zero — \(\sum(x_i - \bar{x}) = 0\).
(2) Median — the middle value when data are sorted from smallest to largest.

If n is odd: median = the value at position \(\dfrac{n+1}{2}\).
If n is even: median = average of values at positions \(\dfrac{n}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{n}{2}+1\).

The median is resistant to extreme values (outliers). Use it for skewed distributions such as income or housing prices.
(3) Mode — the value(s) that appear most often. A dataset can be unimodal, bimodal, or have no mode.


Measures of Dispersion
(1) Range = Largest value − Smallest value. Simple to compute but sensitive to outliers.
(2) Variance — average squared deviation from the mean. We square the deviations so that positive and negative errors do not cancel out:
\[\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum(X_i - \mu)^2}{N} \quad \text{(population variance)}\]
\[s^2 = \frac{\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n-1} \quad \text{(sample variance)}\]
Why n − 1 for samples? Dividing by n − 1 (Bessel’s correction) adjusts for the fact that a sample systematically underestimates the true population spread when you use \(\bar{x}\) instead of the unknown \(\mu\).
A computationally handy equivalent for the numerator is the sum of squares (SS):
\[SS = \sum x_i^2 - \frac{(\sum x_i)^2}{n} \quad \Rightarrow \quad s^2 = \frac{SS}{n-1}\]
(3) Standard deviation — square root of variance, in the same units as the original variable:
\[\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2} \qquad s = \sqrt{s^2}\]


The Empirical Rule
For a bell-shaped (symmetric) distribution, approximately:



Interval
% of observations




\(\mu \pm 1\sigma\)
~68%


\(\mu \pm 2\sigma\)
~95%


\(\mu \pm 3\sigma\)
~99.7%





z-Scores
A z-score (standardized value) tells you how many standard deviations an observation is above or below the mean:
\[z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} \quad \text{(population)} \qquad z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s} \quad \text{(sample)}\]
z > 0 means the value is above the mean; z < 0 means below. Values with |z| > 3 are often considered outliers.

section: Chapter 4: Describing the Relation between Two Variables
text:
Chapter 4: Describing the Relation between Two Variables

What This Chapter Is About
Does more irrigation water mean higher yields? Does fertilizer price affect application rate? Scatter plots, correlation, and simple linear regression answer these questions.


Scatter Diagrams
A scatter diagram plots each observation as a point (x, y). By convention: - The independent (explanatory) variable x goes on the horizontal axis. - The dependent (response) variable y goes on the vertical axis. - Do not connect the points — each point is a separate observation.
The pattern reveals the direction (positive / negative / none) and form (linear / curved) of the association.


Linear Correlation Coefficient
The linear correlation coefficient r measures the strength and direction of the linear association between two quantitative variables:
\[r = \frac{\sum xy - \dfrac{(\sum x)(\sum y)}{n}}{\sqrt{\left(\sum x^2 - \dfrac{(\sum x)^2}{n}\right)\left(\sum y^2 - \dfrac{(\sum y)^2}{n}\right)}}\]
Properties of r:



Value of r
Interpretation




r = +1
Perfect positive linear association


r close to +1
Strong positive linear association


r ≈ 0
Little or no linear association


r close to −1
Strong negative linear association


r = −1
Perfect negative linear association



Important: r is unitless — it does not change if you rescale x or y. Correlation measures only linear association; a strong curved relationship can give r ≈ 0.


Least-Squares Regression
The least-squares regression line \(\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x\) minimizes the sum of the squared vertical distances (errors) between the observed values y and the predicted values ŷ.
Formulas for the coefficients:
\[b_1 = \frac{\sum xy - n\bar{x}\bar{y}}{\sum x^2 - n(\bar{x})^2} \quad \text{(slope)}\]
\[b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1\bar{x} \quad \text{(intercept)}\]
Interpretation: - b₁ (slope): for each 1-unit increase in x, the predicted y changes by b₁ units (on average). - b₀ (intercept): predicted y when x = 0. This is meaningful only if x = 0 is within (or close to) the observed range of the data.


Coefficient of Determination
\[R^2 = r^2 = \frac{\text{Explained variation in } y}{\text{Total variation in } y}\]
R² is the proportion of the total variation in y that is accounted for by the linear relationship with x. For example, R² = 0.87 means 87% of the variation in yield is explained by irrigation water; the remaining 13% is due to other factors (soil quality, weather, etc.).
Scope of the model: use the regression line to predict y only for x-values within (or very close to) the range of observed x. Extrapolating far beyond the data is unreliable because the linear relationship may not continue.

Chapter 5: Probability

What This Chapter Is About
Probability underpins all of statistics. Excel lets you compute empirical probabilities directly from data using COUNTIF and build contingency tables with PivotTables.


Key Excel Skills



Task
Excel Tool / Function




Count outcomes meeting a condition
=COUNTIF(range, criteria)


Count with two conditions
=COUNTIFS(r1, c1, r2, c2)


Compute a proportion
= count / COUNTA(range)


Complement rule
= 1 - P(A)


Contingency table
Insert → PivotTable





Step-by-Step: Empirical Probability from Data
Suppose you have 300 farm records. Column A = Irrigation (Yes/No); Column B = Above-Average Yield (Yes/No).

=COUNTIF(A2:A301, "Yes") → farms using irrigation.
=COUNTIFS(A2:A301,"Yes", B2:B301,"Yes") → irrigated farms with high yield.
Divide each count by 300 for probabilities.
Conditional probability: P(High Yield | Irrigation) = P(Both) / P(Irrigation).



Constructing a Contingency Table
Insert → PivotTable with Irrigation as rows, Yield Category as columns, and Count of farms as values. Row and column totals give marginal probabilities.


Checking Independence
Two events A and B are independent if P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Compute both sides in Excel and compare.

Chapter 6: Discrete Probability Distributions

What This Chapter Is About
Some outcomes are counts: diseased plants per field, farms applying for a subsidy, defects per harvest batch. The binomial and Poisson distributions model these. Excel has built-in functions for both.


Key Excel Skills



Task
Excel Function




Binomial P(X = k)
=BINOM.DIST(k, n, p, FALSE)


Binomial P(X ≤ k)
=BINOM.DIST(k, n, p, TRUE)

Expected value (discrete)
=SUMPRODUCT(values, probabilities)





Step-by-Step: Binomial Distribution
An extension survey finds 40% of small farms adopt a new pest-control method. You sample 10 farms. P(exactly 4 adopt)?

=BINOM.DIST(4, 10, 0.4, FALSE) → 0.2508
P(at most 4): =BINOM.DIST(4, 10, 0.4, TRUE) → 0.6331
P(more than 4): =1 - BINOM.DIST(4, 10, 0.4, TRUE) → 0.3669



Building a Probability Distribution Table

Column A: k values 0 through 10.
Column B: =BINOM.DIST(A2, 10, 0.4, FALSE) dragged down.
Insert a Bar Chart of columns A and B to visualize the distribution.
Check: =SUMPRODUCT(A2:A12, B2:B12) should equal n × p = 4.



Poisson Distribution
A field averages 3 pest infestations per season. P(X = 5)?

=POISSON.DIST(5, 3, FALSE) → 0.1008
P(X ≤ 5): =POISSON.DIST(5, 3, TRUE) → 0.9161

Chapter 7: The Normal Probability Distribution

What This Chapter Is About
The normal (bell-shaped) distribution is the cornerstone of statistical inference. Crop yields, soil nutrient levels, and many economic variables follow approximately normal distributions.


Key Excel Skills



Task
Excel Function




P(X ≤ x) for normal distribution
=NORM.DIST(x, mean, sd, TRUE)


Find x given P(X ≤ x) = p
=NORM.INV(p, mean, sd)


Standardize: z = (x − μ) / σ
=STANDARDIZE(x, mean, sd)


P(Z ≤ z) standard normal
=NORM.S.DIST(z, TRUE)


Find z given probability
=NORM.S.INV(p)





Step-by-Step: Computing Normal Probabilities
Wheat yields: μ = 45 bu/acre, σ = 8 bu/acre.

P(X < 50): =NORM.DIST(50, 45, 8, TRUE) → 0.7340
P(X > 55): = 1 - NORM.DIST(55, 45, 8, TRUE) → 0.1056
P(40 < X < 55): =NORM.DIST(55,45,8,TRUE) - NORM.DIST(40,45,8,TRUE) → 0.6540



Finding a Percentile
What yield marks the 90th percentile?
=NORM.INV(0.90, 45, 8) → 55.25 bu/acre


Drawing the Bell Curve in Excel

Column A: x values from 13 to 77 in steps of 1 (=SEQUENCE(65, 1, 13, 1) in Excel 365, or type manually).
Column B: =NORM.DIST(A2, 45, 8, FALSE) dragged down.
Insert a Line Chart using columns A and B. This draws the bell curve for your distribution.



Checking Normality
From the Descriptive Statistics output (Chapter 3): Skewness near 0 and Excess Kurtosis near 0 suggest normality. A skewness above 1 or below −1 indicates significant departure from normality.

Chapter 8: Sampling Distributions

What This Chapter Is About
A statistic like the sample mean x̄ is itself random — it changes with each new sample. Its sampling distribution describes that variability and is what makes confidence intervals and hypothesis tests valid.


Key Concepts
The Central Limit Theorem (CLT): For large enough n, the distribution of x̄ is approximately normal with mean μ and standard error σ/√n — regardless of the population’s shape.


Step-by-Step: Simulating the CLT in Excel

In Sheet1, column A (rows 1–1000): enter =RANDBETWEEN(1, 100) for a uniform “population.” Freeze values (Copy → Paste Special → Values).
In Sheet2, create a 200-row × 30-column table. Each cell: =INDEX(Sheet1!$A$1:$A$1000, RANDBETWEEN(1,1000)) — this draws 30 random values per row (200 samples of n = 30).
In column AE of Sheet2: =AVERAGE(A2:AD2) for each row — these are 200 sample means.
Build a Histogram of those 200 means. Even though the population was uniform (flat), the histogram of means looks approximately bell-shaped — that’s the CLT.



Standard Error

SE = σ/√n (if population SD is known)
SE ≈ s/√n (estimated from sample)
From Descriptive Statistics output: the Standard Error row gives s/√n directly.

Larger n → smaller SE → narrower sampling distribution → more precise estimates.

section: Chapter 9: Estimating the Value of a Parameter

Chapter 9: Estimating the Value of a Parameter

What This Chapter Is About
We rarely know the true population mean μ. A confidence interval uses sample data to estimate a plausible range for μ with a stated level of confidence (90%, 95%, or 99%).


Key Excel Skills







Task
Excel Function / Tool




Margin of error (σ unknown, use t)
=CONFIDENCE.T(alpha, stdev_s, n)


Margin of error (σ known, use z)
=CONFIDENCE.NORM(alpha, sigma, n)


t critical value (two-tailed)
=T.INV.2T(alpha, df)


z critical value
=NORM.S.INV(1 - alpha/2)


Full CI from ToolPak
Descriptive Statistics → check Confidence Level





Step-by-Step: 95% CI for Mean Yield
Sample: n = 36 farms, x̄ = 48 bu/acre, s = 10 bu/acre.

SE = = 10 / SQRT(36) → 1.667
t* (df = 35, two-tailed) = =T.INV.2T(0.05, 35) → 2.030
Margin of error = = 2.030 * 1.667 → 3.38
CI: (44.62, 51.38) bu/acre

Or use the shortcut: =CONFIDENCE.T(0.05, 10, 36) returns the margin directly.

Chapter 10: Hypothesis Tests Regarding a Parameter

What This Chapter Is About
Hypothesis testing is the formal framework for deciding whether data gives enough evidence to reject a claim about a population. Is average farm income above $50,000? Has a new fertilizer pushed average yield beyond 45 bu/acre?


Key Excel Skills



Test
Excel Tool

= (xbar - mu0) / (s / SQRT(n))


p-value (two-tailed)
=T.DIST.2T(ABS(t_stat), df)


p-value (right-tailed)
=T.DIST.RT(t_stat, df)


p-value (left-tailed)
=T.DIST(t_stat, df, TRUE)

=T.INV.2T(alpha, df)

Chapter 11: Inference on Two Population Parameters

What This Chapter Is About
You often want to compare two groups — irrigated vs. non-irrigated farms, organic vs. conventional yields, income before and after a policy change.

Chapter 12: Additional Inferential Methods

What This Chapter Is About
This chapter covers the chi-square test for categorical data and extends linear regression to formal inference — testing whether predictors are significant and building prediction intervals.


Part A: Chi-Square Tests







Task
Excel Function

Step-by-Step: Test of Independence
Question: Is crop type independent of farm size?

Build a 3×2 observed table from your data using COUNTIFS.
Compute expected frequencies: E = (Row Total × Column Total) / Grand Total for each cell.
=CHISQ.TEST(observed_range, expected_range) → returns the p-value directly.
df = (rows − 1)(columns − 1). Compare p to α = 0.05.

When comparing means across three or more groups — four fertilizer rates, three irrigation methods — use ANOVA instead of running multiple t-tests (which inflates Type I error).
